responses.rationale: The snippet shows og_image_url.html_safe inside a quoted content="..." attribute, so ERB escaping is deliberately disabled (sink present). There is no evidence of how og_image_url is constructed or whether an attacker can inject quote/angle-bracket characters into it. Without source and attacker-control evidence, XSS via attribute breakout cannot be established or ruled out.

The redis service (and neighboring services in the same compose file) has no security_opt: no-new-privileges. That is a real container-hardening gap. The surrounding file is clearly a local/dev stack (Vite dev server, empty Postgres password, host-published ports). Absence of privilege restriction here is not an application exploit path that is operationally actionable in this engagement.

verified_dimensions.sink: missing no-new-privileges on the redis service definition

responses.rationale: The hit is available_locales_with_name.to_json.html_safe embedded into a widget bootstrap script. The value is locale catalog metadata serialized with to_json, then marked safe so JSON is not HTML-escaped. The packet does not show that this structure is attacker-influenced user content; it is application locale enumeration. The claimed XSS path via this specific expression is not supported.

The finding cites “unscoped find,” but the code is Current.account.inboxes.find(params[:inbox_id]) followed by authorize @inbox, :show?. Lookup is tenant-scoped through the current account’s association, then authorized. The unscoped cross-tenant Model.find(params[:id]) mechanism is not present.

On update, password is taken from validated_data and applied with instance.set_password(password) with no validate_password(...) (or equivalent) in the method. DRF validated_data does not, by itself, run Django AUTH_PASSWORD_VALIDATORS. The packet establishes set-without-validator for a password field on a user serializer path.

verified_dimensions.sink: set_password(password) without validation call in evidence

responses.rationale: The base service anchor has no read_only: true (writable container filesystem). That is a real compose hardening observation, in a development-oriented compose (RAILS_ENV: development, local image tags). It is not an in-app vulnerability path that is operationally actionable here.
Same pattern as #1278: @inbox = Current.account.inboxes.find(params[:inbox_id]) then authorize @inbox, :show?. Find is account-scoped and authorized, not a global unscoped lookup.

path.join(c.modRequest.platformProjectRoot, "app/src/main/res/xml") runs inside an Expo Android config plugin at build time. The second segment is a string literal; the first is the tooling project root, not request/user path input. No path-traversal attacker source is shown.

HttpResponseForbidden(_("Insufficient permissions.")) returns a fixed, translated string. The XSS concern for raw HttpResponse requires putting untrusted content into the body; the packet shows only a constant message, not user-controlled HTML.

path.join(xmlDir, "network_security_config.xml") joins a previously constructed build directory with a literal filename, then writes a constant XML template. No user-controlled path component is in the packet.

src_conn.execute(_V1_SELECT) sits in a vector-store migration (m0001_v1_to_v2.py) with fixed schema SQL and a named select constant. There is no request handler or attacker-supplied query fragment. This is offline migration code, not a reachable SQLi surface.

The loop walks nested settings for a read (getSettingRawValue). Before descending, each segment must pass isSafeObjectKey(keyPart) and Object.prototype.hasOwnProperty.call(settingObj, keyPart). There is no assignment into arbitrary keys that would set __proto__ / constructor.prototype. Prototype-pollution write is blocked by the shown guards; the loop does not merge untrusted objects.

The evidence is only import importlib.resources. That is a language/compatibility import, not a security mechanism (no injection, auth, or data-flow issue). Even if flagged as a Python 3.7 compatibility note, it is not operationally actionable as a vulnerability.

verified_dimensions.sink: none for a security issue; plain stdlib import

responses.rationale: self._conn.execute("DROP TABLE IF EXISTS " + DEFAULT_TABLE_NAME) concatenates a DEFAULT_* identifier into static SQL. The packet does not show user or request input in that name; surrounding methods use the same fixed vector-store schema helpers. SQL injection via attacker-controlled table name is not established.

A non-literal RegExp is built with `${key}`, which can be risky if key is attacker-controlled. The only call site in the packet is getForwardedHeaderValue(req.headers.forwarded, "host"), so key is the literal "host". The Forwarded header is the subject of the match, not the pattern. Pattern injection via this evidence is not established.

verified_dimensions.attacker_control: key is literal "host" at the shown call site

responses.rationale: console.error(`[trial-worker] Failed ... user ${user.id}`, err) is a template literal plus a separate error argument. It is not a printf-style format string where attacker input is the format. No unsafe format-string mechanism is present.

Inside a WebView HTML/script template, const initialReaderStyles = JSON.parse(${initialStyles}); interpolates initialStyles into a script context. Nearby, content is passed through escapeForInlineScript, and title is HTML-escaped, but the packet does not define how initialStyles is built or escaped. Sink-like embedding is visible; source, escaping, and attacker control are not.

console.error(`Error persisting client (payload ${json.length} chars):`, e) interpolates a numeric json.length into a template literal and logs an error object as a second argument. That is not an unsafe format-string / format-injection pattern.
